x1vsckxs.author: Plato
x1vsckxs.label: Suddenly, a beauty with no form
x1vsckxs.translation: He who has been instructed thus far in the things of love, and who has learned to see the beautiful in due order and succession, when he comes toward the end will suddenly perceive a nature of wondrous beauty ... or in the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the bodily frame, or in any form of speech or knowledge, ... but beauty absolute, separate, simple, and everlasting,
x1vsckxs.reading: She calls this "a wonderful non-dual description": Diotima cannot describe the final beauty because it is ineffable, so she approaches it by negation (no face, no hands, no speech, no knowledge). This beauty is what is beheld in awakening. She attaches to it the phrase κάλλος ἀμήχανον, beauty without any "mechanism" or mode, which in Plato's text is actually spoken by Glaucon of the Good (Republic 509a).

x118xcqf.author: Plato
x118xcqf.label: The ascent of eros to the sea of beauty
x118xcqf.translation: and first, if he be guided by his instructor aright, to love one such form only--out of that he should create fair thoughts; ... in the next stage he will consider that the beauty of the mind is more honourable than the beauty of the outward form. ... until he is compelled to contemplate and see the beauty of institutions and laws, ... and after laws and institutions he will go on to the sciences, that he may see their beauty, ... drawing towards and contemplating the vast sea of beauty, he will create many fair and noble thoughts and notions in boundless love of wisdom;
x118xcqf.reading: In her retelling the ladder rises from bodily attraction to the attraction of souls, then political eros (falling in love with society, its laws and institutions), the eros of the sciences and of the arts, and finally divine eros, merging into the ocean of life. The "sea" is where knowledge must let go and dive.

x1a4j5wt.author: Plato
x1a4j5wt.label: Beauty shining in pure light
x1a4j5wt.translation: There was a time when with the rest of the happy band they saw beauty shining in brightness,--we philosophers following in the train of Zeus, others in company with other gods; and then we beheld the beatific vision and were initiated into a mystery which may be truly called most blessed, ... which we beheld shining in pure light, pure ourselves and not yet enshrined in that living tomb which we carry about, now that we are imprisoned in the body, like an oyster in his shell.
x1a4j5wt.reading: She cites the Phaedrus for the ineffable luminosity that is the goal Plotinus calls "the View": θεωρία, which she derives from θεός and ὁρῶ, "I see the god". It is ἄρρητον because words work in duality.
